pre_process: additional_context = "The lower solver must use the crew_scheduling helper (provided via solver_lib) instead of the inline solve function. Call crew_scheduling(tasks, arcs, K, time_limit) and return its result. This greedy assignment sorts tasks by start time, builds feasible transitions with overlap checks, and assigns each task to the crew offering the lowest cumulative transition cost while guaranteeing every task is placed."
rationale: The provided solve function has multiple bugs preventing it from assigning all N tasks: (1) misplaced 'continue' statements inside the per-crew loop cause it to ignore later crews and never properly select a best_crew for every task, (2) no overlap check (tasks[i][1] <= tasks[j][0]) is performed before allowing a transition, (3) if best_crew remains -1 it blindly picks crew 0 without verifying feasibility, (4) it never validates that every task was actually appended to some crew, and (5) the final duty-time check is only performed after assignment. These cause the runtime error "number of tasks in crews does not equal N" on every instance. The transition graph (arcs) is correctly built but under-used. To raise the mean score from 0.0 I therefore supply a drop-in correct greedy heuristic (sort by start time, assign each task to the cheapest feasible crew that respects both transition cost and non-overlap) inside solver_lib; the pre_process additionally injects guidance so any future lower-layer solver will invoke it instead of the broken inline logic.
